name: Aon plc
headquarters: Registered office 15 George's Quay, Dublin 2, Ireland D02 VR98 (about 29,000 sq ft, lease to 2044); the largest offices are 165 Broadway, New York (204,000 sq ft) and 200 East Randolph Street, Chicago (191,000 sq ft), with 122 Leadenhall Street, London at 178,000 sq ft. The company does not use the phrase 'operational headquarters' in its filings, so both the Irish registered office and the far larger US offices are stated rather than adjudicated
employees: Approximately 60,000 employees in more than 120 countries as of 31 December 2025 (FY2025 10-K)
summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Aon is the world's second-largest insurance broker and, on the evidence of this research, the leader in the one market this corpus most cares about — its Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program quadrupled from USD 1.5bn to USD 5bn in twelve months, ahead of every competing facility, and it has placed what it calls the first-ever data-centre-specific reinsurance treaty aligning up to USD 5bn of capital behind a single insurer. Nine days before this dossier it agreed to buy USI for USD 17.0bn in cash, all debt-funded, which takes leverage to about 4.8x — above the roughly 3x at which S&P said it would consider a downgrade — with buybacks paused, earnings dilution through 2027, and an interim chief financial officer in post since 17 August 2026. BACKGROUND. Irish-domiciled and NYSE-listed, about 60,000 employees in more than 120 countries. FY2025 revenue USD 17,181m, up 9 percent with 6 percent organic growth — ahead of Marsh McLennan's 4 percent — adjusted operating margin 32.4 percent and adjusted EPS USD 17.07. Two reportable segments: Risk Capital (USD 11,290m — Commercial Risk Solutions USD 8,497m, Reinsurance Solutions USD 2,793m) and Human Capital (USD 5,907m — Health Solutions USD 3,839m, Wealth Solutions USD 2,068m). GAAP net income rose 39 percent, but that is the USD 1,199m gain on selling the majority of NFP's wealth business, not operations. Total debt fell from USD 17,016m at end-2024 to USD 14,967m at 30 June 2026 before the USI commitment reversed the deleveraging. Collection gaps: the company publishes no leverage ratio or debt-to-EBITDA target; no first-party founding date or merger history appears in the FY2025 filing; and its only published battery-storage capacity figure is an eight-year-old regional brochure claim.
ecosystemRole: The second incumbent of this corpus's insurance-and-risk-transfer segment, and the one whose published position sits closest to the AI build-out itself. Like Marsh McLennan it is a broker rather than a carrier — the 10-K states the strategy plainly as focusing 'on higher-margin, capital-light professional services businesses', which is why its energy and digital-infrastructure vehicles are facilities assembled from other people's capacity rather than delegated underwriting on its own paper. That is the structural line between it and kWh Analytics: kWh is a managing general agent that binds risk, Aon is the channel that reaches it, and this research found no evidence of Aon operating a renewables or storage managing general agency of its own. Its distinctive contribution here is capital assembly for data centres — a USD 5bn multi-line lifecycle facility, a first-of-its-kind data-centre reinsurance treaty, and a stated ability to structure individual projects to USD 13-15bn using alternative capital — set against a battery-storage record that is real but thin: one documented first-of-its-kind UK storage placement, a named seat on the challenger's broker council, and published guidance that names engineering criteria but no standard.

productsAndServices.name: Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program — and the first data-centre reinsurance treaty
productsAndServices.description: A multi-line facility covering a data centre from construction through operations, elevated into the 10-K's own business description — a rare signal of where the company wants its growth story read. The filing calls it a programme 'designed to support data center projects from construction through ongoing operations by bringing together traditionally fragmented risk classes into a single coordinated insurance solution'. Alongside it, and separate from it, the chief executive's shareholder letter records the placement of a first-ever data-centre-specific reinsurance treaty.
highlights: Capacity quadrupled in twelve months: USD 1.5bn at launch on 9 July 2025, USD 2.5bn on 14 January 2026, USD 3.5bn on 15 April 2026 and USD 5bn on 20 July 2026

At USD 5bn the tower is construction all risks, delay-in-start-up and property damage and business interruption up to USD 5bn; third-party liability USD 200m outside the United States and USD 100m within it; cyber and technology errors and omissions USD 400m; project cargo USD 500m; terrorism USD 1bn — all on A-rated or higher security across Lloyd's and company markets

The structural feature that matters for a project financing: 'seamless cover with explicit embedded commissioning coverage, and automatic delay-in-start-up sum reduction as phases go live' — the company has solved for phased energisation in data centres in a way its battery guidance has not

THE FIRST-EVER DATA-CENTRE REINSURANCE TREATY, from the chief executive's shareholder letter: 'designing and placing the first-ever data center-specific treaty, aligning up to $5 billion of capital behind a single leading insurer while also engaging other markets to expand capacity for clients'. This is a second and separate USD 5bn — a retail facility and a reinsurance treaty behind a carrier
Management stated at Q2 2026 that it can now support individual projects up to USD 13-15bn using alternative capital sources, and that the data-centre pipeline is three times the prior year
Reinsurance Solutions held 5 percent organic growth in Q2 2026 despite a 15 to 20 percent decline in reinsurance treaty rates, with management citing data-centre new business as the offset
productsAndServices.positioning: On construction capacity this is the largest facility any broker has named: USD 5bn against Marsh's Nimbus at USD 2.7bn and Willis's USD 3bn. Joe Peiser, chief executive of Risk Capital: 'Digital infrastructure has become one of the most important and capital-intensive asset classes in the global economy.' The competitive answer from Marsh came on the operational side, with Stratus, rather than by matching the construction number.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Retail broking into the facility, placed through the company's Global Broking Centres in London, Bermuda and Singapore, with the reinsurance treaty executed through Reinsurance Solutions.
productsAndServices.roadmap: The 'Reliable by Design' approach was announced with the July 2026 expansion; no further capacity step or line extension has been published.

productsAndServices.name: Commercial Risk Solutions
productsAndServices.description: The largest solution line at USD 8,497m of FY2025 revenue: insurance and specialty broking, global risk consulting, captives management and affinity programmes. The 10-K describes it as using 'Risk Capital's extensive data and analytics capabilities to provide brokerage and consulting services that help organizations develop, improve, and implement their risk management strategies', organised around industry and product 'including but not limited to property, casualty, financial and professional lines, construction, transportation, energy, cyber, surety, trade credit, crisis management, transaction liability, and climate'.
highlights: FY2025 revenue USD 8,497m, up 8 percent with 6 percent organic growth; Q2 2026 USD 2,295m, up 5 percent with 5 percent organic
Energy is named as one of the organising verticals in the 10-K itself, alongside construction and climate

Reaches the market through the Global Broking Centres in London, Bermuda and Singapore and through proprietary facilities including the Aon Client Treaty, which the 10-K describes as giving clients access to capital 'regardless of insurance carrier, placement structure or geography'
The only solution line to beat consensus organic growth in Q1 2026 — 7 percent against 5.6 percent expected, while Reinsurance, Health and Wealth all missed
productsAndServices.positioning: Unlike Marsh McLennan, this company names its competitors in its own filing: 'Marsh McLennan, Willis Towers Watson, Arthur J Gallagher & Company, and Lockton Companies, Inc.', plus insurers that market directly without brokers. It does not name Alliant, Brown & Brown, AmWins, McGriff or CAC Specialty.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Retail broking and advisory, with placement through the Global Broking Centres and into proprietary facilities. The company is a large captive manager but this research found no evidence it operates a renewables or storage managing general agency on its own paper.
targetSegments: Large corporate and multinational risk buyers
Middle-market businesses through NFP and, on completion, USI
Energy, construction and digital-infrastructure project sponsors
productsAndServices.roadmap: Totalis Specialty Group was announced on 25 August 2026 to launch on 1 January 2027. Aon DPX, a digital placement exchange, was announced on 18 May 2026.

productsAndServices.name: Reinsurance Solutions — including Aon Securities
productsAndServices.description: Treaty and facultative reinsurance broking, the Strategy and Technology Group, and a capital-markets arm the 10-K describes without hedging as 'a global investment bank with expertise in insurance-linked securities, capital raising, strategic advice, restructuring, and mergers and acquisitions'. FY2025 revenue USD 2,793m. This is the line through which the data-centre treaty was placed, and the line whose rates are falling fastest.
highlights: FY2025 revenue USD 2,793m, up 5 percent with 6 percent organic growth; ranked first globally among reinsurance brokers on FY2024 revenue at USD 2.656bn — but overtaken by Guy Carpenter in H1 2025, USD 1.877bn against USD 1.952bn, and no source located reports the FY2025 outcome
The top tier of this company, Marsh Re, Gallagher Re and Howden Re holds more than 85 percent of reinsurance premium per The Insurer — 'roughly six out of every seven dollars'

Aon Securities' twentieth annual insurance-linked securities report (28 August 2026): alternative capital USD 144.5bn, catastrophe-bond issuance USD 24.9bn, outstanding catastrophe bonds USD 63.4bn, sidecars USD 23bn, 78 sponsors including 16 first-timers, investor return 12.5 percent
Modelling tools named in the 10-K: Capital Insights Explorer, ReMetrica and PathWise
Held 5 percent organic growth in Q2 2026 against a 15 to 20 percent fall in treaty rates — the data-centre treaty is what management credited
productsAndServices.positioning: The capital-markets arm is what distinguishes this line from a pure broking desk, and it is the mechanism behind the claim that individual data-centre projects can be structured to USD 13-15bn. Where Marsh Re's September 2026 publications name battery storage and solar zero times, this company's reinsurance arm is the one that placed a purpose-built treaty for the asset class this corpus tracks.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct broking to insurance and reinsurance carriers, with capital-markets execution through Aon Securities as a broker-dealer.
productsAndServices.roadmap: Aon Securities forecasts catastrophe-bond issuance above USD 20bn for a second consecutive year in 2026.

productsAndServices.name: Power, Renewables and Energy Transition
productsAndServices.description: The practice through which this company meets batteries and renewables. The power practice claims 'more than 300 power and utility specialists worldwide' and the renewables practice states the company is 'the risk manager and broker to over 1,000 renewable energy projects globally' with 'an integrated team of specialists across broking, risk, engineering, claims, and advisory'. Battery energy storage is named on both pages as a covered technology.
highlights: Sub-sectors named on the renewables page: biomass, geothermal, hydroelectric, onshore wind, offshore wind, solar, wave and tidal, green hydrogen, battery storage, pump storage, and carbon capture and storage; the power page adds gravity storage

Products named: property damage, machinery breakdown, forced outage, business interruption, natural catastrophe, parametric, general liability, delay in start-up, advance loss of profit, contractors all risks, erection all risks, pandemic, political violence and cyber, plus risk engineering, captive studies and claims recovery consulting

DOCUMENTED BATTERY PLACEMENT: on 7 July 2026 Pulse Clean Energy reached financial close on two UK battery projects at Plymouth and Dowlais backed by Ariel Green's Technology Performance Insurance offering up to 13 years of protection, with this company as broker — described as the first such policies placed for energy storage projects in the UK market

A Cyber Property Damage Facility offering 'up to $50M (with additional capacity available if required)' for property damage and business interruption arising from malicious cyber acts, explicitly pitched at battery-storage owners

COLLECTION GAP: the only megawatt-scale battery figure the company publishes — '+150MW BESS projects insured' — comes from an Australia and Pacific brochure coded June 2018 that also states 'more than 72,000 colleagues' against about 60,000 today. No current global battery portfolio figure, project count or premium is published anywhere located
productsAndServices.positioning: Its published battery guidance is broker-engineering-led rather than standards-referenced. It asks for 'three metres or more of spacing to mitigate the risk and spread of fire' where 'developers... specify only two metres'; it warns that 'the current fire protection systems can do more damage and cause more losses in BESS than a fire itself'; and it states the underwriting problem plainly — 'there is little in the way of claims data for BESS that are plugged into the grid, unlike comparable renewable technologies such as wind or solar'. Across every battery and renewables publication reviewed it names no UL 9540A, NFPA 855, DNV, TUV, CSA or IEC; the single standard it cites is SCOR's 2022 handbook. Marsh McLennan's guidance does the same, so this is a feature of broker-authored guidance rather than of one firm.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Retail broking and advisory, into facilities assembled from carrier capacity. No renewables or storage managing general agency on own paper was found — the contrast with kWh Analytics, which holds delegated authority, is structural rather than one of scale.
targetSegments: Renewable energy developers, utilities and independent power producers
productsAndServices.roadmap: The Low-Carbon Transition Framework for Insurers, launched 17 November 2025, forecasts energy-transition premiums above USD 9bn by 2030, battery storage above USD 1bn of gross written premium by 2027 at about 25 percent compound growth, hydrogen at USD 5bn by 2027, and renewable power insurance up about USD 3bn globally between 2024 and 2030. These are the company's own forecasts, published to help carriers size the market rather than as a commitment of its own capital.

productsAndServices.name: NFP, and the USI acquisition — the middle market
productsAndServices.description: The middle-market platform. NFP, acquired for about USD 13bn in April 2024, is not a reporting segment: its revenue is absorbed into the solution lines and it runs as a distinct client-facing brand with its own bolt-on programme. On 30 August 2026 the company agreed to acquire USI Advantage Corp. from KKR and other shareholders for USD 17.0bn in cash — the largest acquisition in its history, agreed thirteen days after its chief financial officer left.
highlights: USI: 'the tenth largest U.S. insurance broker with approximately $3 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,500 team members across nearly 200 U.S. offices', headquartered in Valhalla, New York

Price USD 17.0bn, or USD 16.7bn net of about USD 278m of tax attributes — about 14.5 times synergized trailing-twelve-month adjusted EBITDA, or roughly 22 times pre-synergy — funded with new debt across a range of maturities, subject to downward adjustment for leakage since 30 June 2026

Synergies of USD 395m of annual run-rate net adjusted EBITDA, phased USD 92m in 2027, USD 310m in 2028 and USD 373m in 2029; accretive to adjusted EPS only in 2028; integration and transaction expenses about USD 710m plus up to USD 400m of retention incentives over three years

Leverage expected to reach about 4.8x at closing against a 2.8-3.0x target, returning to target in about 24 months, with share repurchases paused; the company expects to maintain Baa2 with Moody's and A- with S&P

Mike Sicard, USI's chairman and chief executive, becomes President of Aon plc and global chief executive of Middle Market. Closing expected in Q4 2026; the parties are not required to close before 19 October 2026 and the outside date is 1 June 2027, extendable twice by three months for regulatory approvals
The management structure came first: Doug Hammond became Global Executive Chairman of Middle Market on 19 August 2026, twelve days before the deal was announced

The substantial majority of NFP's wealth business was sold to Madison Dearborn Partners, agreed 3 September 2025, producing a USD 1,199m gain and more than USD 2bn of proceeds — which is why Wealth Solutions revenue prints minus 18 percent while running 3 to 5 percent organic
productsAndServices.positioning: This is the second debt-funded middle-market acquisition in thirty months, into a market Marsh McLennan entered with McGriff at USD 7.75bn. On Business Insurance's 2025 brokerage-revenue basis it takes this company from about USD 16.99bn toward about USD 19.9bn against Marsh McLennan's USD 26.66bn — narrowing a gap that has been stable for over fifteen years, and widening the one Gallagher has been trying to close from third.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Retail agency distribution across US offices, with USI adding wholesale and excess-and-surplus capability and its own USI One analytics platform.
targetSegments: US middle-market businesses — a segment the company sizes above USD 40bn and at more than a third of US commercial property and casualty premium
productsAndServices.roadmap: Closing expected Q4 2026 subject to regulatory approvals. No financing announcement, bridge facility or notes offering had been published as at 9 September 2026.

productsAndServices.name: Health Solutions and Wealth Solutions
productsAndServices.description: The people half of the firm: health and benefits consulting and broking, consumer benefits, compensation and talent advisory on one side; retirement consulting, pension administration, pension risk transfer and investment consulting on the other. FY2025 revenue USD 3,839m and USD 2,068m. Not risk transfer for physical assets, and included here because the 10-K's Human Capital segment is a third of the company and because Health and Wealth are where its organic growth is genuinely weak.
highlights: FY2025 organic growth of 5 percent in both lines, but Q1 2026 missed consensus in both — Health 4 percent against 5.3 percent expected, Wealth 1 percent against 2.9 percent
Health Solutions organic growth decelerated to 2 percent for FY2025 from 6 percent in both Q2 and Q3 2025, attributed to slower discretionary spend in talent solutions and delayed closed sales
Wealth includes pension risk transfer, delegated and outsourced chief investment officer mandates, master trusts and pooled employer plans; the pooled employer plan passed USD 5bn in August 2025
Benefits programme design is delivered across more than 120 countries with a proprietary digital enrolment platform
productsAndServices.positioning: If a criticism of this company's organic growth is to be made, this is where it belongs — not in the consolidated number, which at 6 percent for FY2025 beat Marsh McLennan's 4 percent and every major listed competitor except Lockton.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Consulting and broking engagements, with NFP as the middle-market benefits channel.

productsAndServices.name: Analytics, AI platforms and published market research
productsAndServices.description: The analytics layer the company presents as its differentiation, delivered through Aon Business Services, plus the research it publishes to set the terms of the markets it brokers.
highlights: Named platforms: the Risk Analyzer family, with Property Risk Analyzer cited on the digital-infrastructure page; Aon Inpoint for insurer-facing analytics; Climate Risk Monitor, upgraded to version 3.0 on 7 May 2026 to quantify extreme heat and cooling demand; and the Resilience Quotient risk-maturity diagnostic

AI launches through the window: Aon Broker Copilot (23 June 2025), Claims Copilot (11 November 2025, expanded globally 13 May 2026), Contract AI for reinsurance coverage analysis (16 June 2026), an AI Risk Diagnostic (27 July 2026) and Aon DPX, a digital placement exchange (18 May 2026)

Published data-centre research with dated figures: data-centre energy consumption from 82 GW in 2025 to 220 GW by 2030; more than USD 1.3 trillion of global data-centre investment over five years; 165 percent projected growth in global data-centre power demand by 2030; data centres at about 11 percent of US power demand by 2030; water use from 560 billion litres a year to 1.2 trillion by 2030

The battery-to-data-centre bridge, stated by the company itself: 'Solar + Battery Storage: Supports peak shaving and sustainability objectives while enhancing grid resilience', with five named insurance consequences including stranded-asset risk from speculative grid applications, bridge power during interconnection delays, and that 'data centers must be insured as utilities with distinct underwriting approaches'

Sam Beaver, Power Leader in the Global Broking Centre, on interdependency: 'Power, cooling and control systems are increasingly interdependent, creating pathways for rapid fault propagation. Critical risks include coolant distribution failure, electrical instability within inverter-based systems, shared infrastructure faults, battery thermal events and control system errors'
productsAndServices.positioning: The research is the clearest first-party evidence in this corpus that a broker has connected the data-centre build to the storage and generation behind it — a connection Marsh McLennan makes through its power practice but not in its published battery guidance.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Bundled with broking and consulting engagements; the research is published free as an agenda-setting instrument.
targetSegments: Insurers and reinsurers, through Aon Inpoint
productsAndServices.roadmap: Aon Business Services is the stated vehicle for accelerating NFP onto a common platform and for further AI deployment; 2026 is the final year of the three-year 3x3 Plan.

relationships.note: Holds a named seat on kWh Analytics' Renewable Energy Broker Council in both published years, represented both times by the same person — the only firm on the council with that continuity.
relationships.context:
John Katilus represents the company in the 2025 readout (Insurance Journal, 2 July 2025) and again in the 2026 readout (pv magazine USA, 9 June 2026). His 2025 contribution is the single most-cited battery observation in this corpus: 'Aon's claims team has seen a small number of hot commissioning losses of Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) farms.' His 2026 contribution is a coverage-wording argument — that clients want the severe convective storm definition narrowed to exclude straight-line wind, tornado and lightning, because grouping them with hail overstates loss potential.

The relationship is distribution rather than rivalry, and the structural difference matters: kWh Analytics holds delegated underwriting authority and binds carrier paper, while this company is capital-light by stated strategy and assembles facilities from other people's capacity. This research found no evidence it operates a renewables or storage managing general agency of its own. That is why the challenger seats it on its council rather than competing with it.

relationships.note: The other incumbent in this segment — second to it on every published revenue ranking for more than fifteen consecutive years, ahead of it on data-centre capacity and on organic growth, and adverse to it in court.
relationships.context:
AM Best's 2025 ranking puts Marsh McLennan first at USD 26.98bn against this company at USD 17.20bn, a gap of about USD 9.8bn, and Business Insurance ranks them first and second in both its global and its US-business tables. The measure is contested: Marsh McLennan's total bundles consulting revenue that is not broking, and AM Best's own 2018 table showed this company larger on a broking-only basis. No source published since offers a clean broking-only comparison.

On the two measures that matter to this corpus the ranking inverts. Organic growth for FY2025 was 6 percent here against Marsh McLennan's 4 percent. And on data-centre construction capacity this company's facility reached USD 5bn in July 2026 against Nimbus at USD 2.7bn, plus a first-of-its-kind data-centre reinsurance treaty; Marsh McLennan's answer came on the operational side with Stratus in August 2026.

They are also litigants. Marsh USA sued this company and Robert McDonough in federal court in New York in April 2025 after twenty employees resigned within a 38-minute window, McDonough becoming chief executive of its North American construction, infrastructure and surety group seven days later. It declined to comment.

relationships.note: Adjacent seats at the same financial close rather than a commercial relationship — and the same documented absence found on the other incumbent's side.
relationships.context:
DNV certifies and writes recommended practice for grid-scale storage, including RP-0043; this company advises the buyer and places the risk. The DNV dossier in this corpus records that it found no insurer document citing RP-0043 or naming any certifier.

This research corroborates that from the other direction. Across every battery and renewables publication reviewed here — the two UK battery articles, the energy-transition roadmap, the clean-energy-lifecycle article, the renewable construction claims analysis, the Asia-Pacific construction-to-operations piece, the power and renewables capability pages and the Spring 2026 market update — no UL 9540A, NFPA 855, DNV, TUV, CSA or IEC reference appears. The single standard cited anywhere is SCOR's 2022 handbook. What substitutes for a named standard is qualitative engineering criteria: three metres of enclosure spacing, wind-turbine fleet-leader operating hours, OEM facility provenance. Marsh McLennan's guidance does the same across seven documents. Two incumbent brokers, independently, state the requirement and leave the code unnamed.

policyExposure.regime: Irish domicile and OECD Pillar Two
policyExposure.exposure: The 10-K states the company is 'subject to income taxes in Ireland, the U.K., the U.S., Singapore and many other jurisdictions' and could be taxed more heavily 'as a result of changes in eligibility for the benefits of current income tax treaties'. On Pillar Two it is specific: the OECD's 15 percent country-by-country minimum tax has been enacted by 'Ireland, the U.K., Singapore, and many E.U. member states', the company's net income 'is subject to the 15% minimum tax in countries that have enacted Pillar Two, and in Ireland (Aon's parent company location) with respect to countries that have not enacted a qualifying minimum tax', and there remains 'significant uncertainty as to how Pillar Two applies to Aon in prior years'. The GAAP effective tax rate was 21.2 percent in FY2025 against 21.4 percent in FY2024.

policyExposure.regime: Irish corporate law and enforcement of judgments
policyExposure.exposure: A distinct risk factor states that 'We are incorporated in Ireland, and Irish law differs from the laws in effect in the U.S. and may afford less protection to holders of our securities', and that 'It may not be possible to enforce court judgments obtained in the U.S. against us in Ireland' because 'the U.S. currently does not have a treaty with Ireland providing for the reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments'. Distributions to shareholders require distributable profits obtained through intercompany dividends or a reduction in share capital 'approved by the High Court of Ireland' — a structural constraint on the buyback and dividend policy that a US-incorporated peer does not carry.

The most directly relevant risk factor in this dossier, because it is the risk of having nothing to broker: 'If access to underwriting markets for certain lines of coverage becomes unavailable or difficult due to the impact of climate change on the claims environment, this may have a negative impact on our clients' access to coverage, which could in turn reduce our ability to place certain lines of coverage and negatively impact our business.' A companion sentence states that 'Climate change may increase the likelihood or severity of a natural or human-caused disaster.' Battery storage and utility-scale renewables sit inside exactly that exposure — the company's own battery guidance records that capacity 'is... limited' and that grid-connected storage has 'little in the way of claims data'.

policyExposure.regime: Artificial intelligence regulation and AI operational risk
policyExposure.exposure: The 10-K names 'additional requirements related to the use of artificial intelligence, and the use, access, privacy, protection, management, localization and transfer of data' as a compliance burden, and carries a separate operational risk factor: the company 'continue[s] to invest in artificial intelligence, particularly in generative artificial intelligence tools', and certain use cases 'could pose strategic, operational, legal, ethical, regulatory' risks 'where there is inadequate human oversight'. AI also appears as a competitive threat — 'new and non-traditional competitors (including InsurTech firms utilizing artificial intelligence or other emerging technologies)' — which the market priced on 9 February 2026 when broker shares fell across the sector on an AI-native comparison app.

policyExposure.regime: Antitrust — the terminated Willis Towers Watson combination
policyExposure.exposure: The 2021 attempt to combine with Willis Towers Watson, at about USD 30bn, was abandoned on 26 July 2026 to end Department of Justice litigation, with a USD 1bn termination fee paid. The European Commission had granted conditional approval on 12 July 2021 subject to divestitures to Arthur J. Gallagher, and Turkey and South Africa had cleared it; the DOJ alone stopped it. In the FY2025 10-K the matter survives in only two places — WTW as a named competitor, and an interest accrual for income tax reserves 'related to the termination fee payment made in connection with the Company's terminated proposed combination with Willis Towers Watson'. No WTW-specific antitrust risk factor remains. The precedent is still cited as the benchmark for broker-deal scrutiny, and it is the reason the USI acquisition's regulatory path is worth watching.

policyExposure.regime: Data protection, sanctions and financial crime
policyExposure.exposure: The 10-K enumerates the perimeter in one paragraph: businesses are 'subject to extensive legal and regulatory oversight throughout the world, including the Irish Companies Act, the U.S. securities laws... the rules and regulations promulgated by the FCA and a variety of other laws' addressing 'licensing, data privacy, data management and data protection, artificial intelligence, trade sanctions laws, restrictions and export controls, anti-money laundering... antitrust and competition, anti-corruption'. Named extraterritorial statutes: the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, FATCA, the UK Bribery Act 2010 and the EU General Data Protection Regulation. The company transacts inside sanctioned-adjacent theatres with government support — a USD 25m war-risk facility for Ukraine with KNIAZHA Vienna Insurance Group and the US Development Finance Corporation was announced on 9 February 2026.

policyExposure.regime: SEC enforcement — Aon Investments USA and the PSERS matter
policyExposure.exposure: In January 2024 the SEC charged Aon Investments USA Inc., formerly Aon Hewitt Investment Consulting, and a former partner with misleading the Pennsylvania Public School Employees' Retirement System about discrepancies in investment-return calculations. It settled for a USD 1m civil penalty plus USD 542,187 of disgorgement and prejudgment interest. A Fair Fund distribution plan was approved by SEC order on 7 April 2026, so the matter remains live administratively. Separately, the company recognised USD 197m of legal settlement expense in Q4 2023 over transactions where capital was arranged by Vesttoo, primarily involving letters of credit alleged to be fraudulent; its Bermuda segregated-account vehicle White Rock sued China Construction Bank in August 2024 seeking at least USD 140m, and that litigation was still live in 2026.

strategyRead: 1. **(High confidence)** We assess that this company is an incumbent of the insurance-and-risk-transfer segment, and specifically the second incumbent rather than a co-equal of the first. Basis: AM Best has ranked it second globally on broker revenue for more than fifteen consecutive years, at USD 17.20bn for 2025 against Marsh McLennan's USD 26.98bn; Business Insurance ranks it second both globally and among the largest brokers of US business; and its reinsurance arm was first globally on FY2024 revenue inside a top four holding more than 85 percent of reinsurance premium. The gap to first is about USD 9.8bn and has been stable for over a decade. The corpus should not present the two incumbents as equals.

2. **(High confidence)** We assess that this company currently leads the market this corpus exists to track, and that the lead is in data centres rather than in storage. Basis: its Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program went from USD 1.5bn to USD 5bn in twelve months — larger than Marsh's Nimbus at USD 2.7bn and Willis's USD 3bn — with a published multi-line tower, embedded commissioning cover and automatic delay-in-start-up reduction as phases energise. Separately, the chief executive's shareholder letter records placing 'the first-ever data center-specific treaty, aligning up to $5 billion of capital behind a single leading insurer'. Management states it can structure individual projects to USD 13-15bn using alternative capital, and that its data-centre pipeline is three times the prior year. The 10-K elevated the facility into its own business description, which no other product receives.

3. **(High confidence)** We assess that neither incumbent broker in this segment anchors its battery-storage guidance to a named standard, and that this is a property of broker-authored guidance rather than of one firm. Basis: across every battery and renewables publication reviewed for this dossier — two UK battery articles, the energy-transition roadmap, the clean-energy-lifecycle article, the renewable construction claims analysis, the Asia-Pacific construction-to-operations piece, the capability pages and the Spring 2026 market update — no UL 9540A, NFPA 855, DNV, TUV, CSA or IEC reference appears; the single standard cited anywhere is SCOR's 2022 handbook. What substitutes is qualitative engineering criteria: three metres of enclosure spacing against the two developers specify, wind-turbine fleet-leader operating hours, OEM facility provenance. Marsh McLennan's guidance does the same across seven documents. Two incumbents, independently, state the requirement and leave the code unnamed.

4. **(High confidence)** We assess that the USI acquisition is the dominant fact about this company for the next two years and that it reverses its own recently completed deleveraging. Basis: leverage peaked at 3.7x after NFP, was brought to 2.8x by September 2025 and 2.5x pro forma for the NFP wealth proceeds, earning an S&P outlook revision to stable on 14 November 2025 at A-/A-2 — with a stated downgrade trigger of leverage sustained at about 3x. The USD 17.0bn all-debt USI purchase takes leverage to about 4.8x at closing, pauses buybacks, defers adjusted-EPS accretion to 2028, and carries about USD 710m of integration and transaction expense plus up to USD 400m of retention incentives. The company expects to hold Baa2 and A-; neither agency had published a view as at 9 September 2026.

5. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess that the structural difference between this company and the segment's challenger is delegated authority, not scale, and that it is the reason they are partners rather than rivals. Basis: the 10-K states the strategy as focusing 'on higher-margin, capital-light professional services businesses', and every energy and digital-infrastructure vehicle located is a facility assembled from carrier capacity rather than delegated underwriting on own paper. kWh Analytics, by contrast, binds risk under delegated authority. This research found no renewables or storage managing general agency operated by this company. That is why the challenger seats it on its own broker council. Confidence is moderate because managing general agency arrangements are frequently unpublicised, so absence of evidence is weaker here than usual.

6. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess that its battery-storage franchise is real but thin, and that the dossier should not inflate it. Basis: one documented placement — Pulse Clean Energy's Plymouth and Dowlais projects on 7 July 2026, backed by Ariel Green Technology Performance Insurance for up to thirteen years and described as the first such policies placed for UK energy storage — plus a named council seat and substantive published guidance. Against that: the only megawatt-scale battery figure it publishes comes from a brochure coded June 2018 that also states a headcount half again its current one; no current global battery portfolio figure, project count or premium exists; its most quantified renewables claims analysis breaks out wind at 83 percent, hydro at 10 percent and solar at 7 percent and excludes storage entirely; and it is not named at all in the most substantive independent renewables-pricing article of 2026.

7. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess that the common criticism of this company's organic growth is misdirected, and that the real weakness is in Human Capital. Basis: FY2025 organic growth was 6 percent against Marsh McLennan's 4 percent, Gallagher's 6 percent and WTW's 5 percent — ahead of every major listed competitor except Lockton at 13 percent. Insurance Journal made the comparison explicitly on the day of the print. The weakness is elsewhere: Health Solutions organic decelerated to 2 percent for FY2025 from 6 percent in both Q2 and Q3 2025, and Wealth Solutions grew 1 percent in Q1 2026 against 2.9 percent expected. Three of four solution lines missed consensus organic growth that quarter; only Commercial Risk carried it.

8. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess that the adjusted-versus-GAAP gap and the cash-flow reversal are the numbers a reader should watch rather than the headline beats. Basis: the company has beaten adjusted EPS by a hair and missed revenue in three consecutive prints — Q4 2025 adjusted EPS beat 2.11 percent on a 1.83 percent revenue miss, Q2 2026 adjusted EPS beat by a single cent on a 0.47 percent revenue miss and a 10.8 percent GAAP EPS miss. Free cash flow fell 34 percent in Q2 2026 against full-year guidance of double-digit growth. FY2025's 39 percent net income increase is a disposal gain. None of this is deterioration on its own, but the adjusted line is doing more work than usual.

9. **(Low confidence)** We assess that the sequence of the chief financial officer's departure and the USI announcement is worth watching but does not yet support an inference. Basis: Edmund Reese left effective immediately on 17 August 2026 'to pursue opportunities outside the firm', an interim was appointed the same day from the corporate planning function, guidance was reaffirmed, and thirteen days later the company committed USD 17.0bn of new debt. No source connects the two events, no explanation for the departure has been published, and no permanent appointment has been announced. Sources also disagree on when Reese became chief financial officer — 2022, 'two years ago', or July 2024. The sequence is recorded; the inference is not drawn.

10. **(Low confidence)** We assess that the AI-disintermediation repricing of February 2026 was directionally right about the mechanism and wrong about the timing. Basis: an AI-native insurance comparison app took this company's shares down 9.3 percent and WTW's down 12 percent in a single session, with Bank of America sizing about USD 15bn of low-complexity commissions at risk; three research houses called it overdone because the product was personal lines while the majors are commercial. The company's own 10-K names 'InsurTech firms utilizing artificial intelligence' as competitors and flags AI use cases as an operational risk 'where there is inadequate human oversight'. Its answer is to build the tools itself — Broker Copilot, Claims Copilot, Contract AI, an AI Risk Diagnostic and a digital placement exchange, all launched inside fourteen months.

A rating action from Moody's or S&P on the USI financing. S&P's stated downgrade trigger is leverage sustained at about 3x; the deal takes it to about 4.8x. The company expects to hold Baa2 and A-. Whichever way this resolves, it settles Judgment 4.
The financing itself: a bridge facility, a commitment letter or a notes offering. As at 9 September 2026 none had been published for a USD 17.0bn all-debt purchase.
A permanent chief financial officer. An appointment, and any explanation of the August departure, would close the open question in Judgment 9.

Q3 2026 results, expected around 30 October 2026 (unconfirmed — six consecutive Friday prints ended when Q2 2026 landed on a Wednesday). Watch whether Reinsurance Solutions holds 5 percent organic against still-falling treaty rates, and whether Health and Wealth recover.
Any published battery-storage capacity figure, project count or premium that is not the 2018 brochure. Its absence is currently the strongest evidence for Judgment 6.
A second documented battery placement. One first-of-its-kind UK deal is a franchise only if it repeats.

Regulatory review of the USI acquisition. The 2021 Department of Justice challenge that killed the Willis Towers Watson combination — at a USD 1bn termination fee — is the benchmark commentators still apply, and Gallagher's AssuredPartners deal drew a second request in March 2025. No second request on USI had been reported nine days in.
